title: Wet readings
prompt: The flood team studies every reading where rain fell. Write `solve(observations)` so it returns the `observation_id`, `station_id`, `observed_at` and `precipitation_mm` of the readings with rain that weren't flagged suspect.
rules: Rain fell when `precipitation_mm` is more than 0.0. A reading of exactly 0.0 was dry.
NaN in `precipitation_mm` is a gauge fault, not rain, so leave it out. An empty value is left out too.
Leave out readings whose `quality_flag` is `suspect`. A reading with no flag at all stays in.
Return the four columns in that order, duplicates included.
hints: Try `F.col("precipitation_mm") > 0` on its own and look at the result: a NaN reading is there. Spark treats NaN as larger than every number.
Add `~F.isnan("precipitation_mm")` to shut out the faulty readings. An empty value already fails `> 0`.
`quality_flag != "suspect"` isn't true for an empty flag, so that row would vanish. Keep it with `F.col("quality_flag").isNull() | (F.col("quality_flag") != "suspect")`.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(observations):
    # Return the rainy readings that weren't flagged suspect.
    return observations
explanation: Two different kinds of missing value pull in opposite directions. NaN is a real value, and Spark sorts it above every number, so `precipitation_mm > 0` is true for a faulty gauge; `~F.isnan("precipitation_mm")` removes it. A null is the other way round: a comparison with it isn't true, so an empty rain value drops out by itself, but so does an empty `quality_flag` under `!= "suspect"`, which is why the flag check needs `isNull() |`. Together: `observations.filter((F.col("precipitation_mm") > 0) & ~F.isnan("precipitation_mm") & (F.col("quality_flag").isNull() | (F.col("quality_flag") != "suspect"))).select("observation_id", "station_id", "observed_at", "precipitation_mm")`. `observations.dropna(subset=["precipitation_mm"])` before the filter also works, because `dropna` counts NaN as missing.
